text.p: Polish computer maker Optimus SA will consider selling shares to a foreign strategic investor once its convertible bonds are converted into stock, the company's president told the daily Parkiet on Friday.

"In the case of the conversion of the convertible bonds into shares the firm will have serious financial partners among its shareholders. So now we can talk about a potential foreign strategic investor," Parkiet quoted Roman Kluska as saying.
Each of the firms' 300 five-year $100,000 convertible bonds is exchangeable into 6,947 common shares at 38.76 zlotys a share before the bonds mature on June 20, 2001.
The stock closed at 61 zlotys on Thursday.
Kluska said 87.5 percent of the bonds were taken up buy foreign investors which he would not name, save for the issue's underwriters, Merrill Lynch and Bank Pekao SA.
He said the firm had already invested a third of the $30 million gained from the issue, which in two years would allow the firm to cover its liabilities from the issue.
He said the remaining $20 million went to bank deposits and could be invested immediately after the bond conversion.

Kluska also said the firm would have to form provisions concerning the issue which would be made up for in earnings by tax refunds, the liquidating of previous provisions, and a dividend from subsidiary Optimus IC.
He said the latter sources of funds could allow the firm to net twice as much in 1997 as previously forecast.
In October last year the company expected to earn 10.7 million zlotys in 1997's first half.
